title: Impact of Paid Family Leave on Women's Labor Force Participation

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Difference-in-Differences (TWFE). States that adopt paid family leave (treated) are compared to states that do not (controls) before and after implementation (post).
- Why: The policy varies across states and time; DID with state and period fixed effects removes time-invariant state heterogeneity and common time shocks.
- Key assumptions:
  - Parallel trends: In the absence of the policy, treated and control states would have had parallel trends in women’s labor force participation.
  - No spillovers: Policies in treated states do not affect outcomes in control states.
  - No anticipatory effects: Outcomes do not change in treated states before the policy due to anticipation.
  - Stable composition/measurement over time.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(lmtest)
  library(sandwich)
})

# 1) Read data
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s42_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Sanity checks
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    unit_id = as.integer(unit_id),
    period = as.integer(period),
    treated = as.integer(treated),
    post = as.integer(post),
    treat_x_post = as.integer(treat_x_post)
  )

# Verify interaction term consistency; if inconsistent, reconstruct
if (any(df$treat_x_post != df$treated * df$post)) {
  warning("treat_x_post does not equal treated*post; reconstructing.")
  df <- df %>% mutate(treat_x_post = treated * post)
}

# Basic sample info
n_units <- n_distinct(df$unit_id)
n_periods <- n_distinct(df$period)
n_treated_units <- n_distinct(df$unit_id[df$treated == 1])
n_control_units <- n_distinct(df$unit_id[df$treated == 0])

cat("Sample summary:\n")
cat(" - Observations:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat(" - States (units):", n_units, " (treated:", n_treated_units, ", controls:", n_control_units, ")\n")
cat(" - Periods:", n_periods, "\n\n")

# Helper to extract and print estimate for treat_x_post
print_did <- function(model, vc, label = "Model") {
  ct <- coeftest(model, vcov. = vc)
  if (!("treat_x_post" %in% rownames(ct))) {
    stop("Coefficient treat_x_post not found in model.")
  }
  beta <- unname(ct["treat_x_post", "Estimate"])
  se   <- unname(ct["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"])
  tval <- unname(ct["treat_x_post", "t value"])
  pval <- unname(ct["treat_x_post", "Pr(>|t|)"])
  ci_l <- beta - 1.96 * se
  ci_u <- beta + 1.96 * se
  pct  <- 100 * (exp(beta) - 1)
  pct_l <- 100 * (exp(ci_l) - 1)
  pct_u <- 100 * (exp(ci_u) - 1)

  cat(paste0(label, " DID estimate (coef on treat_x_post):\n"))
  cat(sprintf("  beta = %.4f, SE (clustered) = %.4f, t = %.2f, p = %.3f\n", beta, se, tval, pval))
  cat(sprintf("  95%% CI: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", ci_l, ci_u))
  cat(sprintf("  Interpreted as percent change in y: %.2f%%  (95%% CI: [%.2f%%, %.2f%%])\n\n", pct, pct_l, pct_u))
  invisible(list(beta = beta, se = se, ci = c(ci_l, ci_u), pct = pct, pct_ci = c(pct_l, pct_u)))
}

# Cluster-robust variance-covariance (cluster at state level)
vcov_cl_unit <- function(model) sandwich::vcovCL(model, cluster = ~ unit_id, type = "HC1")

# 2) Main DID: Two-way fixed effects (state and period FE)
mod_twfe <- lm(y ~ treat_x_post + factor(unit_id) + factor(period), data = df)
vc_twfe <- vcov_cl_unit(mod_twfe)
res_main <- print_did(mod_twfe, vc_twfe, label = "Main TWFE")

# 3) Classic DID without FEs (adds treated and post directly)
mod_simple <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
vc_simple <- vcov_cl_unit(mod_simple)
res_simple <- print_did(mod_simple, vc_simple, label = "Simple DID (no FE)")

# 4) Robustness: TWFE + differential linear time trend for treated group
#    Allows treated states to have a different linear time trend.
df <- df %>% mutate(t_numeric = as.numeric(scale(period, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE))) # centered time
mod_trend <- lm(y ~ treat_x_post + I(treated * t_numeric) + factor(unit_id) + factor(period), data = df)
vc_trend <- vcov_cl_unit(mod_trend)
res_trend <- print_did(mod_trend, vc_trend, label = "TWFE + treated linear trend")

# 5) Placebo test: use only pre-period data, define a pseudo cutoff within pre and re-estimate DID
df_pre <- df %>% filter(post == 0)
if (nrow(df_pre) >= 10 && n_distinct(df_pre$period) >= 2) {
  pre_periods <- sort(unique(df_pre$period))
  pseudo_cut <- pre_periods[ceiling(length(pre_periods) / 2)]
  df_pre <- df_pre %>%
    mutate(pseudo_post = as.integer(period >= pseudo_cut),
           placebo = treated * pseudo_post)
  mod_placebo <- lm(y ~ treated + pseudo_post + placebo, data = df_pre)
  vc_placebo <- vcov_cl_unit(mod_placebo)
  # Temporarily rename coefficient to 'treat_x_post' for reuse of printer
  ct <- coeftest(mod_placebo, vcov. = vc_placebo)
  beta <- unname(ct["placebo", "Estimate"])
  se   <- unname(ct["placebo", "Std. Error"])
  ci_l <- beta - 1.96 * se
  ci_u <- beta + 1.96 * se
  pct  <- 100 * (exp(beta) - 1)
  pct_l <- 100 * (exp(ci_l) - 1)
  pct_u <- 100 * (exp(ci_u) - 1)
  cat("Placebo DID in pre-periods (coef on treated x pseudo_post):\n")
  cat(sprintf("  beta = %.4f, SE (clustered) = %.4f, 95%% CI [%.4f, %.4f]\n", beta, se, ci_l, ci_u))
  cat(sprintf("  Percent change: %.2f%% (95%% CI [%.2f%%, %.2f%%])\n\n", pct, pct_l, pct_u))
} else {
  cat("Placebo test skipped: insufficient pre-period variation.\n\n")
}

# 6) Also report simple group-by-time mean differences for transparency
agg <- df %>%
  group_by(treated, post) %>%
  summarise(mean_y = mean(y), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = c(treated, post),
                     values_from = mean_y,
                     names_prefix = "treated_post_")
# Compute DID from means if all cells exist
if (all(c("treated_post_0_0","treated_post_0_1","treated_post_1_0","treated_post_1_1") %in% names(agg))) {
  did_means <- with(agg,
                    treated_post_1_1 - treated_post_1_0 - (treated_post_0_1 - treated_post_0_0))
  cat(sprintf("DID from cell means (log points): %.4f  => percent change ~ %.2f%%\n",
              did_means, 100 * (exp(did_means) - 1)))
} else {
  cat("Could not compute DID from means (missing cells).\n")
}
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Paid family leave should improve women’s attachment to the labor force by reducing separation during childbirth and facilitating return-to-work, yielding higher log participation.
- Magnitude: Modest. I expect roughly 0.01–0.03 log points (about 1–3%) increase in women’s labor force participation on average, with CIs that may include zero in small samples. Effects may be stronger for prime-age mothers but attenuated when averaged across all women.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: We compare changes in women's labor force participation in states with and without the law over time.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The implementation of paid family leave laws is associated with an increase in women's labor force participation.
